INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.

This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.

Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:

A Possible Explanation:

The US knew there was a threat to RAF Fairford - that's not in dispute here. The FPCON changes, armed patrol vehicles inside the base and concrete barricades all show that.

It seems possible to me that perhaps these 5 lads (or 8-10 if the eyewitness farmer is correct) were not actually there to attack the base - perhaps (given the fake fuel vans) they were actually in the area trying to steal fuel from local vehicles.

The farmer sees it, calls police. Police (who likely were aware of the USAF concerns) swarm into the area having perhaps not expected the "attackers" so soon. They manage to arrest 5 suspects and treat the 3 vans with every necessary precaution (as they should) - evacuating the neighbourhood, bringing Army EOD in, etc.

The males are initially arrested for Explosives Act offences (pending a safe way to check inside the vans) & go to custody. In the circumstances, further arrested for the Terrorism Act offence. However, after seizing whatever evidence they could (and examining the vans), it looks like police may have determined these aren't the attackers - as I say, potentially fuel thieves in the wrong place at the wrong time?

It's worth noting that if the terrorism act offences were looking likely, police could keep them detained for 48hrs initially before requiring a court to approve a longer period of time. Alternatively under normal arrest powers contained within the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984, they can be held for 24hrs initially (extended to 36hrs under authority of a Police Superintendent if specific requirements are met), and up to 72hrs if a further extension is authorised by a court. Now clearly if they were arrested in the early hours of Sunday morning and conveyed either to a local custody, or a dedicated counter-terrorism custody (likely closest in London), the fact they've been bailed today suggests they've spent at most 24-30hrs in custody before evidential review officers and the Crown Prosecution Service have determined there is insufficient evidence to charge them with an offence right now.

So they bail them with conditions not to contact each other as is normal procedure for vehicle interference/theft offences like that. But police need to download and analyse phones, and anything potentially seized from home addresses in order to ensure no link to the Iranian government or IRGC.

Meanwhile, did the actual planned attack get foiled inadvertently? Perhaps? Trump told the world that the US had been monitoring the "attackers" for some time - I'd suggest that if these lads genuinely were just in the wrong place at the wrong time, the actual suspects are now staying hidden until this all blows over a bit.

Either way, we don't have all the facts and that's part of any criminal or CT investigation - so yes, it sounds bad and arguably CTP could have done a better job of explaining it to the public, but they have to play their cards close to their chest right now in case my guesswork here is right and the suspects are still out there somewhere.

Twelve independent pharmacies in Arkansas sued Express Scripts on September 15. They say the PBM paid them less than their cost for the medicine at least 48,306 times between August 2025 and March 2026.

That's illegal in Arkansas. State law says a PBM can't reimburse a pharmacy below NADAC, the government's weekly benchmark of what pharmacies actually pay to acquire each drug. It's a floor under the ingredient cost. It doesn't even cover the pharmacist, the rent, or the lights.

The state spent years trying to get PBMs to follow it. Bulletins starting in 2021. By April 2024, regulators were processing 1,000 to 1,500 below-cost claims a month. Pharmacies filed about 3,000 complaints that year. A state review found 654 plan reports, covering roughly 340,000 Arkansans, that consistently paid pharmacies below cost. In August 2024 the governor announced per-prescription penalties, including against Express Scripts.

The problem with that system is who does the work. Every underpayment has to be found by the pharmacy, documented with invoices, appealed and tracked. For a shortfall of a few dollars, the labor costs more than the money. Anything the pharmacy doesn't catch, the PBM keeps. The complaint describes it as turning the law into an interest-free option to underpay until caught.

So in 2025 Arkansas passed Act 990, letting pharmacies sue directly for up to $10,000 per violation plus attorney's fees. The court will decide the actual amount. For context, the statutory ceiling on 48,306 claims is north of $480 million.

A few more details from the complaint:

The pharmacies sent written notice in June and offered to meet. Express Scripts didn't respond.

In February, Express Scripts agreed in an FTC settlement to move its standard retail pharmacy model to acquisition cost plus a dispensing fee. The pharmacies say the underpayments continued after that.

In Arkansas, the three biggest PBMs handle 92.9% of Medicaid managed care fills and 78% of Medicare Part D retail fills. There's nowhere else to go.

Express Scripts sits inside Cigna alongside Express Scripts Pharmacy and Accredo, which compete with these same independents for patients.

And the stakes are real. One study found anticonvulsant fills dropped 15.6% after local pharmacies closed, and mail order didn't make up the difference.

IFF's statement on the AI Impact Summit 2026.

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) welcomes the India AI Impact Summit 2026 (February 16-20) as an important platform for global dialogue on, "Artificial Intelligence". We believe the Summit's agenda and framing fundamentally misalign with the lived reality of AI deployment in India, an environment marked by rising digital authoritarianism and the systematic erosion of constitutional protections that are causing demonstrable harm to vulnerable populations. Its official framing centers on “People, Planet and Progress”, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurating and world leaders like France’s President Emmanuel Macron and top tech CEOs (Google’s Sundar Pichai, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, etc.) expected to attend. The Summit's optimistic narrative about AI for development obscures the reality of how its deployment is impacting people in their everyday lives.

The current environment is one of a sharp contraction in civic space, where recent governance proposals on technology have facilitated the expansion of state power that run contrary to the state commitments on fundamental rights and social justice. Today, there exists few organisations in India that work on digital rights and those which are surviving are severely under resourced, suffer from burdensome compliances, growing legal risks and deliberate exclusion from policy making processes. The decline of civil society work is matching the growth of private and public sector capacity to lobby the policy making processes. So, even before a question is prompted, how should Indian civil society engage with the India AI Impact Summit, a predicate and grounded inquiry is, how many independent, Indian civil society groups exist in India that have capacity and can be critical of state policies and practices around AI?

In the recent past, far from fostering accountability, India’s digitisation drive is often used to sidestep constitutional safeguards of transparency, harming communities and individuals. For instance, recent legal changes have weakened the Right to Information (RTI) framework, curtailing citizens’ ability to question power. The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 introduced an amendment (Section 8(1)(j) to the RTI Act) that blocks access to any information labeled “personal information”, allowing officials to deny critical information. Likewise, digitisation of welfare governance has been weaponized to bypass accountability, with digitisation often becoming a gatekeeper and working to the detriment of the poor. A stark development came in December, 2025 when Parliament hastily passed the Viksit Bharat - Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025 (VB-GRAM G), repealing the landmark MGNREGA jobs guarantee program. VB-GRAM G converted a demand driven legal right to work into a discretionary, bureaucratically controlled scheme, undermining decades of workers’ rights. There are references to "AI" within the text of the objects and reasons that are a part of this law.

Beyond this, India's policies on AI also demonstrate a wider embrace of de-regulation narratives to ensure, "innovation". For instance, the Union Budget 2026 unveiled a 20-year tax holiday (until 2047) for foreign firms using Indian data centers, aiming to lure global AI infrastructure. Yet, this policy was formulated with scant regard for its impact on local communities and natural resources. Other recent measures also deserve comment:

Sanchar Saathi : In late 2025, the government ordered smartphone manufacturers to pre-install a government cybersecurity application called Sanchar Saathi on all devices. The app was ostensibly meant to secure citizens’ phones, but the mandatory installation sparked outrage over privacy and surveillance concerns, drawing parallels to spyware abuse.
The ‘Sahyog’ Censorship Portal: In 2024, the Union Home Ministry quietly launched the Sahyog Portal to expedite content-blocking orders on social media and websites. Under this system, law enforcement agencies can flag “unlawful” online content and directly trigger its takedown by internet platforms, all through a centralized interface.
Expansion of NATGRID: Perhaps the most far-reaching is the quiet expansion of NATGRID, India’s National Intelligence Grid. Long conceived as an integrated database for counter-terror investigations, NATGRID has recently morphed into a broad surveillance net. Following a high-level police conference in late November 2025, states were directed to “scale up” NATGRID usage beyond central agencies, even giving police officers at the Superintendent rank access to its vast datasets.
These developments match the increased use of AI technologies in domains of policing and welfare without a clear legal basis and real safeguards.

IFF acknowledges that the India AI Impact Summit 2026 offers a platform for dialogue and a chance for civil society voices to gain visibility on an international stage. We recognize the value in having digital rights perspectives included in global AI governance conversations, indeed, the Summit’s presence in India is an opportunity to spotlight our constitutional concerns before a world audience. We support our peer organizations and allies who choose to engage with the Summit, and we will remain in constructive collaboration with them. However, IFF has decided not to allocate significant organizational resources to direct participation in the Summit’s events. This is not a boycott of the forum, but a practical choice of focus. As a small team of only 7 full-time staff based in New Delhi, we must prioritize the most pressing advocacy initiatives that align closely with our mission and charter.

This includes ongoing efforts such as legal challenges to unconstitutional regulations, campaigning and community engagement for strengthening free expression, privacy and transparency frameworks. These are battles immediately affecting citizens’ rights and requiring our sustained attention. IFF will engage with the Summit in a mindful, critical manner. We will track the proceedings and outcomes closely, offering our analyses and critiques rooted in constitutional values. If and where we do participate (for example, in side events or discussions), we will do so with a critical gaze, centering the lived experiences of Indians and the paramountcy of our fundamental rights. Our support is firmly with the broader civil society coalition pushing for AI governance that is accountable and just.

#CONSTITUTIONALPOSITION

1. The Election Commission of India is a constitutional authority functioning under Article 324 of the Constitution of India.The Commissioners of the Election Commission are given security of tenure and other safeguards by the Constitution and law.

2. The actions of the Election Commission are subject to judicial review within the limits of the Constitution and the law. However, the electoral roll, election process and election results are not ordinarily open to challenge except in the manner provided by law.

3. The Hon’ble Supreme Court exercises jurisdiction under Article 32 for enforcement of fundamental rights and under Article 136 through special leave petition. Judicial review can be exercised only on limited grounds such as violation of the Constitution, violation of law, mala fides, arbitrariness or exercise of power beyond jurisdiction.

4. The Hon’ble Supreme Court cannot directly inquire into or investigate the Election Commission or its Commissioners. A direct investigation against the Commissioners is not permissible except under the specific provisions of the Constitution and the law.

5. Any complaint against the Chief Election Commissioner or an Election Commissioner can be considered only in accordance with the constitutional procedure provided under Article 324(5) read with the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Conditions of Service) Act, 1991 and the rules made thereunder.

6. The removal of the Chief Election Commissioner can be made only in the same manner and on the same grounds as a Judge of the Supreme Court under Article 124(4) and Article 124(5). The removal of an Election Commissioner can be made only on the recommendation of the Chief Election Commissioner under Article 324(5).

7. Therefore, any investigation or inquiry against the Election Commission or its Commissioners can be undertaken only in accordance with the above constitutional provisions and the relevant law.

8. The Hon’ble Supreme Court can examine the legality and constitutionality of the actions of the Election Commission within the permissible limits of judicial review. However, a direct investigation against the Commission or its Commissioners is not permissible except under the specific constitutional and statutory provisions referred above  only.

India has quietly frozen Starlink. It issued the license nearly a year ago, then let the final security clearance sit, and the whole satellite-comms sector has slowed with it. Indian Express went so low that they have to lie about technicalities of how an API is used. Don't they have educated people on the IT team of Indian Express? Let me expose some of the claims of Indian Express here.

“Meta plugged its API into Sahyog so posts vanish with no human review” mixes up two completely different systems.

The public Meta API (Graph / Instagram Platform) is what developers and AIs actually get. With a token you can hide comments on your own professional account, block someone from your business inbox, or publish your posts. You cannot delete another person’s Reel, geo-block a URL in India, or mass-remove content. There is no public endpoint for that. App Review will not give it to you.

What IE described is a private government–platform pipe, authorised officers put URLs on Sahyog under IT Act 79(3)(b). Meta’s internal compliance stack restricts those URLs, usually for India, under the 3-hour rule. Court filings called this “API-based integration.” Same English word. Not the same API. You cannot call it with an access token.

Also sloppy on units:
  
1.95 lakh is orders, not posts. One order can cover many URLs.

PIB later said ~2.98 lakh URLs. Different count.

“Blocked from Instagram” is often geo-restriction in India, not a global delete. Users have seen Account Status say the post meets Community Standards while India still can’t open it. That is local-law restriction, not Meta’s spam model.

So government notices at this volume + a machine path to meet a 3-hour deadline = a real policy story.

“An AI can automatically block Instagram content with the Meta API” = false. That capability is not in the developer docs, and treating Sahyog as Graph API is how this thread oversells the tech.

If the claim is “takedowns scaled up,” argue that with orders vs URLs and 79(3)(b) vs 69A. Don’t sell it as a public API anyone can point at a meme.

In Portland, Oregon, there’s a small coffee shop called Cozy Bean.

During the day, it’s what you’d expect—people stopping in for a hot drink, soft background music, the usual warmth of a neighborhood café.

But something unexpected happens after closing time.

Once the customers leave and the lights are turned off, the owner turns them back on—but not for more business. He opens the doors again, this time for a different kind of guest: street dogs.

Since 2018, Cozy Bean has quietly offered shelter to stray dogs in the area. There's no advertising, no big signs, no posts asking for attention. It’s just something the owner does—every single night.

Inside, he sets out old blankets, cushions, and bowls of clean water. The dogs come in from the cold, some limping, some soaked from the rain, and they find a place to rest. They aren’t locked in or forced to stay. They just know they’re welcome—and they settle in like they belong there.

Some of the dogs are regulars. Others come and go. But every night, they have somewhere safe to sleep. A break from the noise and danger of the street.
The owner doesn’t do interviews. He doesn’t expect anything in return. He just makes space for those that have none.

It’s a simple act—opening a door, turning on a light, offering a little comfort. But it shows a level of compassion that’s hard to find in today’s world.

This isn’t about saving the world. It’s about doing what you can, right where you are. And that, in its quiet way, is something extraordinary.

Two Muslim women journalists on Thursday alleged that they were beaten by Delhi police personnel in South Delhi’s Saket police station. The two journalists said that a police team detained them and took them to the Saket police station, where they were assaulted.The journalists were on assignment to cover an event attended by Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta and Union Home Minister Amit Shah, following which the assault occurred, the journalists alleged. 

The journalists Shaheen Khan and Nafessa Khan alleged that they were dragged by their hair upstairs and were met with brutish assault for approximately 40 mins. 

“They dragged us upstairs by our hair and brutally assaulted us there. When they became exhausted from beating us, they stopped to take a break.”  Journalist Shaheen Khan told FoEJ Media. 

Both the journalists further claimed that on learning about their Muslim identity, the assault was intensified. 

“When they found out that we were Muslims, she said, ‘You’re Muslim? Now I’ll beat you even more'” Shaheen said. 

“She told me, ‘You’re Muslim? I’ll hit you three or four more times.’ She then struck me so hard with a lathi that the injury is still swollen.”  Nafeesa added, showing her bruises to FoEJ Media. 

Revealing the start of the assault, Shaheen said, “I was standing downstairs, speaking to my family over the phone and informing them about what had happened. Meanwhile, a female police officer approached me and demanded that I hand over my phone. When I told her, ‘Please tell me what happened; whatever you need to discuss, we can discuss it here,’ she replied, ‘I have a different way of talking. We’ll talk upstairs.’” 

“Listen to the language she used. She said, ‘I have a different way of talking. I’ll speak to you upstairs.'” Shaheen highlighted.

“She snatched my phone and started slapping me,” she added. 

Both the journalists further alleged that they were refused to have water even when they were falling to grasp the air due to the continuous assault. 

“When we asked, ‘Ma’am, please give us some water,’ she replied, ‘We will beat you thirsty,'” Shaheen alleged.

“Nafeesa’s condition deteriorated, and she collapsed unconscious. I told them that she needed medical attention, but no one paid any heed,” she added. 

The incident occurred on Thursday morning when the Union Home Minister Amit Shah and Chief Minister Rekha Gupta attended the inauguration of Max Smart Super Speciality Hospital in Saket. 

The journalist said that they had gone to cover the event; however, they were stopped by police and taken to Saket police station, where the assault was launched. 

In an official statement, DCP (South) Anant Mittal described the allegations as “factually incorrect and misleading.”

“Claims suggesting otherwise, including allegations of assault for asking questions to the Hon’ble Chief Minister, are totally false, misleading, and baseless. Citizens and social media users are advised to refrain from circulating unverified and misleading information,” read the statement.  

The police said that despite multiple requests and instructions to remove the vehicles and clear the route, they refused to remove them. Following the security and safety protocol of the VVIP route, both the journalists were taken to the local police station for the inquiry, the police said, and the Hindustan Times highlighted. 

“In recent days, 4pm has been consistently raising serious questions and publishing reports on matters related to the Delhi government and Chief Minister Rekha Gupta. In such a context, it is natural to wonder whether today’s action is connected to those reports and questions in any way.” said Sanjay Sharma, the editor-in-chief of 4pm News Network. 

“Since when has asking questions of the Chief Minister become a crime? Since when has a journalist’s question become so dangerous for those in power? And can a journalist having ‘Khan’ in their name become a reason for assaulting them?” he posted on X. 

In a statement, the Press Club of India, Indian Women’s Press Corps, Delhi Union of Journalists, Press Association, and Kerala Union of Working Journalists condemned the assault and have “called for punitive action against Delhi Police officials…for brutally assaulting [the two] freelance journalists.”

The incident was also condemned by the political leaders. Congress posted the video on X, while members of the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) have condemned the alleged use of force against journalists and accused the government of failing to protect press freedom. Indian Youth Congress leader Darshan Kaushik speaking to FoEJ Media said, “It is extremely shameful that two girls were subjected to brutality after being asked about their religion. text:
So in Delhi, apparently someone can dress up as a policeman and move around without anyone questioning it. Don’t we have to ask how that is possible?

If people allegedly dressed as police officers were able to commit such a serious offence, the question cannot stop at “they were not real policemen.” That answer, if established, raises an even more important question: why was impersonation of police officers possible in the first place, and where were the systems meant to detect it?

A few years ago, after we reported alleged demands for bribes and posted videos, one of my tweets went viral. We were subsequently approached and asked to remove it, with the explanation that the people involved were supposedly “behroopiya log”—impersonators, not police personnel.

I remember thinking then: is this a joke?

And that is why the present incident raises serious questions for me. If individuals dressed as police officers were able to move around and, as reported, assault a woman, the fact that they were allegedly impersonators does not end the accountability question. It begins another one.

Responsibility, however, must be properly assigned.

The park or land-owning authority is generally responsible for the park's maintenance, lighting, access points and any CCTV or security infrastructure under its control, including supervision of contracted services.

The police are responsible for policing, beat patrols, responding to complaints, crime prevention and investigation, and enforcement of criminal law within their jurisdiction.

Civic agencies have responsibility for the civic functions assigned to them, while contractors and security agencies are responsible for the services they have been engaged to provide, subject to oversight by the contracting authority.

Then comes accountability.

If CCTV under an agency's control was not working, who was responsible for maintaining it? Was the failure known? Was it reported? Who was monitoring it?

If a location was known or reported to be unsafe, what preventive measures were available and were they actually being implemented?

If police impersonation was involved, what systems exist to detect and respond to it?

If complaints had previously been made, were they recorded and acted upon?

And if responsibility falls between agencies, who is the nodal authority ensuring that the gap does not become an excuse for inaction?

I have personally encountered situations in South Delhi where I felt complaints received inadequate or delayed attention. I have also raised concerns about alleged demands for bribes. I am describing my experiences and concerns—not claiming that they establish misconduct by an entire institution.

There are many police officers doing difficult work every day. This is not an argument against the police. It is an argument for clear responsibility and measurable accountability.

Citizens, particularly women, should take reasonable precautions. But telling citizens to be careful cannot substitute for functioning public-safety systems.

The questions after an incident should be simple:

Who had the duty? Who was supervising it? Was the risk known? Was it reported? What action was taken? And if the responsibility was not discharged, who was held accountable?

If someone can simply put on a police uniform and walk around Delhi without attracting scrutiny, perhaps the question we should be asking is not merely “Were they really policemen?”

It is: “Why was it possible for them to appear to be?”

Former American senator told to 'cover up' T-shirt during Holyrood tour after flag design seen as 'political' | Daily Mail

A former American senator claims he was told to cover up his T-shirt during a tour of the Scottish parliament after its design was seen as a ‘political statement’.

Republican Scott P. Brown was about to embark on a tour of Holyrood when he says he was stopped by a police officer who took umbrage at his top supporting ‘law enforcement’.

The 67-year-old explained that he had bought the black short-sleeved garment printed with the Thin Blue Line flag, and a Spartan helmet, at a bike festival earlier in the summer.

But posting a video on X, the ex-Massachusetts congressman told his 65,000 followers that he was ‘told to cover up’ after the officer objected to the motifs.

He wrote: ‘Had a great stay in Scotland except when I tried to visit parliament.’ The former senator said in a short clip: ‘This cop came up to me and said “do you mind covering up your shirt”? I’m like what are you talking about? Why? And he says “it’s a political shirt… it represents a political stance’.

Pointing at the blue and white stripes, he tells followers: ‘The political stance is obviously that I support law enforcement, which I do. I was pretty shocked. So we just went in and took off after, because it wasn’t worth it.’ But he still hailed Scotland as ‘a beautiful place’.

It is not the first time visitors have been asked to cover up or remove items due to attire that is seen an inappropriate. In 2024 Jenny Willmott, a co-founder of the campaign group Scottish Lesbians, was told to remove a ‘Scottish Lesbian’ badge at a Women’s Rights Network event due to its ‘partisan message’.

In 2022 the parliament apologised after a woman was ejected for refusing to remove a scarf in the suffragette colours of purple, green and white.

And earlier this year Scottish Greens Maggie Chapman and Kate Nevens were accused of an extremist ‘political stunt’ after wearing pro-Palestine scarves while being sworn in as MSPs.

The Scottish Conservatives said at the time it was ‘blatant hypocrisy’ as Green MSPs previously objected to the women’s rights campaigners wearing suffragette colours in parliament.

The parliament website asks the public to ‘remember that it is a working parliamentary building’ and that ‘protests are not allowed inside the building’.

It advises that visitors are permitted to wear ‘a single small, discreet badge’ to express their view.

But a spokesman said: ‘The Parliament’s visitor behaviour policy prohibits the display of flags, banners and political slogans inside the Holyrood building, including on clothing and accessories.

‘Visitors displaying flags, banners or political slogans are asked to remove or cover up such items before being allowed entry.’

Before action was taken to demolish parts of the Shahi Mosque in Ujjain, Madhya Pradesh, for road widening, the city’s Qazi and mosque officials reportedly asked local residents to leave the area at night by simply saying, “Go back to your homes.” However, they did not clearly inform them that parts of the mosque would be demolished in the morning.

Ujjain/Bhopal:
Tensions had been prevailing in Ujjain since Sunday night over the plan to remove a portion of the Shahi Mosque as part of an ongoing road-widening project being carried out in preparation for the Simhastha Kumbh Mela 2028. Mosque committee members and religious leaders asked the people who had gathered during the night to return to their homes. However, many people alleged that they were not told that the demolition of part of the mosque would begin the following morning.
By morning, a large number of security personnel had been deployed at the site along with the administrative team and police force, and barricades were erected around the mosque. During this time, clashes between some protesters and the police were reported, including allegations of stone-pelting and the use of tear gas.
The administration says that the action to remove the portion of the mosque falling along the proposed route of the widened road is being carried out only after an order from the Madhya Pradesh High Court. The High Court had earlier dismissed two petitions, stating that the municipal corporation had followed due legal procedure.
Meanwhile, a large section of the local Muslim community said that they had merely been told to “go home” during the night, without being given details about the demolition schedule or the broader plan. As a result, many people remained near the mosque until morning, while some even spent the night inside it.

text:
IFF statement against the Alarming Escalation of Social Media Censorship and Proposed Expansion of Takedown Powers

New Delhi, March 19, 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by continuing reports of posts and accounts being withheld in India on Facebook, X and Instagram, including satire and criticism of the government. Recent reporting shows users receiving generic “withheld in India” notices or emails under Section 69A from social media platforms, with little or no explanation, while independent reporting has documented takedowns affecting speech that appears political, satirical, or critical rather than clearly unlawful.

As reported by Business Standard and The Indian Express on March 18, the Union Government is currently exploring a proposal to decentralize content blocking powers under Section 69A of the IT Act. The new proposal would grant direct takedown powers to multiple ministries, including Defence, Home Affairs, External Affairs, and Information & Broadcasting. At present, MeitY signs off on Section 69A orders, while a separate notice and takedown channel already operates through Section 79(3)(b) and the Home Ministry led Sahyog portal that at least has 35 nodal officers across State Police Departments in India.

At the same time, the February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules have sharply compressed compliance timelines. MeitY’s own published FAQ says intermediaries must act within 3 hours when they receive actual knowledge through a court order or a government intimation, within 36 hours for certain expedited grievances, and within 2 hours for specified complaints involving nudity, sexual content, morphed content, and impersonation. The government has also reiterated that intermediaries which fail to observe due diligence risk losing Section 79 immunity. A system built on speed, legal threat, and secrecy predictably incentivises over compliance.

We remind the Union Government that the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A in the Shreya Singhal case on the basis of procedural safeguards and written reasons that could be challenged. Secret and inaccessible censorship defeats those safeguards in practice. 

IFF calls on the Union government to halt any move to decentralise Section 69A blocking powers further, publish blocking orders with only as per the letter and spirit of the Shreya Singhal judgement, and ensure timely notice to affected users with clear grounds and avenues for remedy. Platforms must also do more than send boilerplate messages. They should provide meaningful notice, preserve records for challenge, and publish granular transparency reporting given online censorship also impacts the public right to receive information.

If your account or post has been withheld or blocked in India, please write to legal@internetfreedom.in with screenshots, URLs, and any email or platform notice you have received. IFF will try to assist impacted users and document patterns of opaque censorship.

text:
The Problem: 
How Genuine Voters Get Cheated

In many elections, the winner wins by just a few thousand—or even a few hundred—votes. 

Because the contest is so tight, bad actors use a dirty trick to win: 
Remove genuine voters who might vote against them.

Here is step-by-step how the scam works:

Mass Complaints: 
A party worker sits with a huge list of voters who support opposition parties. 

He fills out hundreds of objection forms (Form 7), lying that these people have moved away or died.

Easy to Lie, Hard to Defend: 
It takes only two minutes to file a fake complaint. 

But for a regular citizen, defending their vote is a nightmare. 

You have to take a day off work, visit a government office, and produce documents to prove you are alive and living in your own house.

Missing Notices: 
By law, the Election Officer (ERO) must send a notice to the voter asking them to appear. 

In reality, these notices often get "lost," delayed, or are never sent at all.

Deleted in Silence: 
When the voter does not show up (because they never received the notice), the officer simply strikes their name off the list. 

The citizen only discovers this on voting day when they are turned away at the booth.

Why People Get Away With It

No Risk, Big Reward: 
The person filing fake forms knows they can steal thousands of votes without getting caught.

Officers Cut Corners: 
Election staff are often under heavy pressure or simply do not bother to check whether the complaint is genuine before deleting a name.

The Practical Solution: 
How Citizens and Social Workers Can Fight Back

The law is clear:
Lying to delete someone’s vote is a serious crime.

Filing a false declaration is an offense under Section 31 of the Representation of the People Act and under criminal laws for fraud and perjury.

Deleting names without proper checking makes the election officer liable for punishment under Section 32 of the same Act for dereliction of duty.

To stop this vote theft, citizens and local workers only need to do two things:

Watch the lists daily: 
Social workers and party agents must check the objection lists at the local election office every day. 

If someone’s name is challenged, go directly to that voter and warn them before the deadline passes.

File police cases against the frauds: 
Don't just complain—file an FIR against the person signing the fake forms, as well as the officer who deleted the name without proper inquiry.

The moment a few fake objectors and careless officers face actual police investigation and jail time, this organized voter fraud will stop immediately.

Burlington vape shop bars unaccompanied women after owner charged with sexual assault: @ScarlettGrace92 

The sex-based policy appeared after the owner of Vape on Plains was charged with sexually assaulting a woman who police say was alone with him at a store location.

A Burlington vape shop barred unaccompanied women from entering the store after its owner was charged with sexually assaulting a woman at one of his store locations.

A notice posted at one of the Vape on Plains locations told customers that, “due to an ongoing situation,” female customers who arrived alone could not be served inside.

Instead, women were instructed to knock on a window where a catalogue of prices and flavours had been provided. Male customers were still permitted inside.

The policy followed the September 8 arrest of 64-year-old Burlington resident Mouhamad “Frank” Sabra, owner of Vape on Plains and Vape on Plains II.

@HaltonPolice allege an adult woman was sexually assaulted after attending the Vape on Plains II location on Plains Road East while she was alone in the store with Sabra.

Sabra was charged with sexual assault and failing to comply with a probation order. The allegations have not been proven in court.

Police also released Sabra’s photograph, saying investigators believe there may be additional victims and asking anyone with information or a similar experience at either store to come forward.

The Plains Road West business had previously run afoul of provincial vaping regulations.

Halton Public Health records show that in March 2023, the business, then listed as “Vape On Plains And Gift Garage,” was convicted of selling a vapour product to someone under 19 and received a $400 set fine.

In May 2026, it was convicted again, this time for offering to sell an improperly packaged vapour product, and fined $365.

Then came a very different controversy. Following the allegation against the owner, it was female customers who found themselves on the other side of the door.

Section 1 of Ontario’s Human Rights Code guarantees equal treatment with respect to services, goods and facilities without discrimination because of sex, raising questions about the legality of treating customers differently based on whether they are male or female.

The notice quickly went viral, with some social media users characterizing the policy as “Sharia law” and even referring to the country as the “Islamic Republic of Canada.”

A subsequent video posted online showed the notice had been removed.

Police have not disclosed the date of the alleged assault or publicly confirmed whether additional alleged victims have since come forward. Their investigation remains ongoing.

text:
Chevonne Rusch was only two years old.

Two.

She should have been learning new words, running around, playing and discovering the world.

Instead, she was beaten to death.

A pathologist later told the court that Chevonne had 49 injuries and bruises across her tiny body. She died from severe bleeding on the brain after head trauma.

Her mother, Rochelle Botha, and Stefan van Niekerk were eventually convicted of her murder, along with a range of other serious offences involving children. Van Niekerk received life imprisonment for the murder, while Botha received 25 years for Chevonne’s murder. Botha’s application for leave to appeal was later refused.

We worked on this case closely during my time at Action Society.

And I still struggle with one simple fact:

Chevonne was two years old.

She could not call the police.

She could not leave.

She could not apply for a protection order.

She depended entirely on adults to notice what was happening and protect her.

They failed her.

When we talk about violence against children, never allow it to become just another statistic.

Remember Chevonne.

Remember 49 injuries on the body of a two-year-old child.

This is why we do what we do. 🙏🏼

text:
The Delhi Police's takedown drive against posts critical of the Prime Minister is unconstitutional. 

New Delhi, 27 July 2026

Media reports today state that the Delhi Police has directed social media platforms to remove posts, videos, memes and reels containing remarks it describes as "abusive", "offensive" and "objectionable" towards the Prime Minister, uploaded during the student protests at Jantar Mantar and after the 'Sansad Chalo' march of 20 July 2026. At least three platforms have reportedly received notices. Several posts have already been taken down. A dedicated police team is monitoring social media to identify further content, and reports indicate that criminal proceedings are contemplated against those who posted it. No order has been published. While reports indicate the notices invoke the Information Technology Act, the specific provision relied upon and the text of the notices remain undisclosed. 

The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns this takedown drive and calls for the notices to be disclosed and withdrawn.

On the reports available, the content being removed is political expression. The movement at Jantar Mantar has been conducted as much through reels, memes, posters and digital artwork as through assembly on the ground. This is how a digital native generation raised online speaks about accountability. As per Article 19(2) restrictions on speech only on eight specified grounds. Offensiveness is not one of them. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the IT Act precisely because expressions such as "grossly offensive" and causing "annoyance" were vague, subjective, and swept protected speech within their net. Eleven years later, the Delhi Police is applying the same standard through informal notices and legal powers which are not being publicly disclosed. 

As per existing practices there are two routes for removing online content. The first is Section 69A of the IT Act read with the Blocking Rules, 2009, which requires a reasoned order, committee review, and notice to the originator, as the Delhi High Court affirmed in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). The second is Section 79(3)(b), which Shreya Singhal read down to require a court order or a government notification strictly confined to Article 19(2) grounds. If these notices were routed through the Sahyog Portal, they rest on a regime whose constitutionality remains under challenge before multiple High Courts. However, even if it is used police notices citing offensiveness satisfy neither. 

Reports that platforms were told the content violates "their policies" make the defect worse, the police have no mandate to enforce the community guidelines of private companies. Unpublished directions are also contrary to Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637, which requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published so that they can be challenged. If the underlying theory is defamation of the Prime Minister, the police have no role at all. Defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognizable offence, prosecuted only on a complaint by the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. 

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must publish every notice issued, the legal provision invoked, and the list of URLs affected.

2. Notices directed at satire, criticism, and political commentary must be withdrawn. Any removal must follow the procedures under Section 69A or a judicial order.

3. No criminal proceedings should be initiated against persons for speech that does not meet the constitutional threshold of incitement.

4. Platforms must decline requests unsupported by valid legal orders, notify affected users, and disclose the number of government demands in their transparency reports.

Students who question an examination system are exercising their fundamental rights and deleting their posts will not delete their questions.

Reports referred to:

1. Times of India, "Delhi Police orders removal of offensive posts against PM Narendra Modi linked to NEET paper leak protests", 27 July 2026
2. News18, "Delhi Police Issues Notices To Social Media Platforms Over Offensive Posts Against PM Modi During Jantar Mantar Protest", 27 July 2026

Most of you want to know what all transpired in between the ‘account withheld in India’ and the final restoration of my account. 

So here’s a quick summary. Please share so that others can take the same recourse, if need be, coz the govt seems in no mood to spare any content critical of it.

On 19th March at 12:23 AM my account was withheld in India.

Very next day, I had a conversation with @SupriyaShrinate and she told me that 12 other accounts met the same fate. She did a live session and addressed media the very same day. That highlighted the issue. The wire, Quint and alt news reported the news.

I swiftly responded to MeitY on 19th March at 4:16 AM enquiring the cause that led to this removal under section 69A. ( Haven’t received any response yet )

Next I consulted with @NakulGandhi511 upon the recommendation of @iArpitSpeaks as he had earlier met with similar fate and got his account back.

Nakul sir guided me for a week and introduced me with @apar1984 who runs @internetfreedom . 

He took over my case pro bono ( for free ) and guided me accordingly. 

On 1st of April I finally filed my writ petition. The notary, wakalatnama was all new to me coz I had never been in court till this date but barring that I had to do nothing. 

Every response, every draft was given to me by @namanbasoyaa who works with Apar sir. 

I got my listing on 6th of April with the honr Judge Purushaindra Kumar Kaurav. 

He didn’t even waste 10 mins and ordered a restore provided that the posts that warranted an action against me shall stay unblocked until the committee level hearing of MeitY ( It’s not scheduled yet )

In fact I still don’t have the blocking order that necessitated such an action against me that is ultra vires of the constitution. Section 69A doesn’t permit govt to remove pre-emotive post based on speculation and that’s exactly what govt effectively did by withholding my entire account not some posts. 

Also big thanks to my followers who stood with me. Some used VPN just to stay connected. I’m indebted to all of you and IFF and Apar sir in particular. 

Taking this opportunity to urge the govt to remove ban from other accounts as well folllwing the same precedence used in mine and @DrNimoYadav ’s case.

FoS needs to be supreme. Taking down post is wrong in itself but an entire account that took years of cultivating is just brutal and uncalled for. 

May better sense prevails. Peace ✌🏽

Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

   - Binance P2P complete order history (screenshots)  
   - Buyer/Seller ke saath chat  
   - Payment proof (UPI, bank transfer screenshot)  
   - Bank statement jisme transaction dikhe  
   - Aadhaar, PAN, Binance account details

3️⃣ Binance Support ko turant contact karo  
   - App mein Help section → Submit ticket  
   - Order ID aur proofs attach karo. Woh counterparty ko investigate kar sakte hain.

 In March 2026, ahead of the Kerala Assembly elections (polling on 9 April 2026), a 2019 Election Commission of India (ECI) letter redistributed by the Kerala Chief Electoral Officer’s (CEO) office was found to carry the seal of the BJP’s Kerala unit. This sparked a political row, followed by police-directed efforts to remove related social media posts

This takedown action itself became controversial, with critics framing it as an attempt to suppress discussion of an official lapse during an election period, while authorities maintained it was necessary to stop the circulation of a withdrawn and erroneous document that was being used to question the ECI’s credibility.The episode remained a flashpoint in the final stretch of the Kerala campaign, with the ECI treating it as a corrected administrative mistake and the opposition presenting it as evidence of deeper concerns about the poll body’s independence.The letter and the seal
The document was an ECI communication dated 19 March 2019 containing guidelines/FAQs on the publicity of candidates’ criminal antecedents (following a Supreme Court judgment). CPI(M) and Congress shared versions online showing the BJP Kerala unit’s seal. It had been circulated by the Kerala CEO’s office to political parties, District Election Officers, and Returning Officers as part of clarifications around mid-March 2026.thesouthfirst.comKerala CEO / ECI explanation:
It was described as a “purely clerical error.” The BJP Kerala unit had approached the CEO’s office seeking clarification on the (by then revised) 2019 guidelines and submitted a photocopy of the original directive that already bore the party’s seal. Staff overlooked this and redistributed that version. The error was identified; on 21 March a formal withdrawal notice was issued telling recipients to disregard the document. An Assistant Section Officer was suspended pending inquiry. Later, a Deputy CEO and a Section Officer were relieved of election-related duties.livemint.comOpposition parties (CPI(M) and Congress) rejected the clerical-error account. They alleged compromised institutional neutrality, claiming seals were being “casually swapped” and questioning whether the ECI and BJP shared the same “power centre.” Some BJP responses labelled the circulation of the old document as misinformation or a political plot.thewire.inDeletion of posts controversyActing on an ECI directive (under the Model Code of Conduct), the Kerala Police cyber cell issued notices to X (Twitter), Facebook, Instagram, and numerous individual accounts. They demanded removal of posts sharing the letter that carried the BJP seal.
